title: Chapter Four: The Tally Does Not Lie

blocks.c: Chapter Four: The Tally Does Not Lie

Captain Ovid Marn was a tall, tired, courteous man who had commanded the Meridian Gull for nine years and had never once, in Sol's hearing, raised his voice — a fact the crew found more alarming than shouting would have been.

He listened to all of it standing up, in the chart room, with his hands behind his back and the cloud going past the windows in long grey rolls. Roake told it. Sol confirmed it. Dov produced two pages of arithmetic which he had done in the eleven minutes since the round, and which Marn read carefully, all the way to the bottom, twice.
Then he said: "Bosun. Your recommendation."

"Ring five rounds a day instead of four until Antrell," said Roake. "Put a hand on the gallery through every watch. Sound the frames hourly. And I want the tally back to the start of the run laid out on that table."
"Granted, granted, granted, and how far back?"
"Eleven years."
Marn's eyebrows went up perhaps a quarter of an inch, which for him was a shout. "That is a great deal of ledger."
"Yes," said Roake.
"Why eleven?"
The bosun did not look at Sol. "Because that is when I first heard it and did nothing about it."
The tally, laid out, filled the chart table and then the floor.

They worked in shifts, because someone still had to run the ship: Sol, Dov, Roake, and — from the second evening, when it became apparent how much ledger there was — Purser Halloway, who was sixty, disapproved of everything, and turned out to be the fastest reader any of them had ever met.

The method was Dov's. For every round in eleven years, take the nine marks. Score them: full is nought, thin is one, dead is three. Add the nine. Write the sum in the margin of a fresh sheet, one line per round, four lines per day.
"You'll get a number that means nothing," said Halloway.
"I'll get a number that means nothing four times a day for four thousand days," said Dov, "and then I'll look at the shape of it, and the shape will mean something, because shapes always do."

It took eleven days to get through it. Sol did her watches, rang her rounds, slept in ninety-minute pieces, and read the handwriting of dead bell-hands until the columns swam. It was tedious in a way she had not known was available. It was also, she admitted to nobody, the happiest she had been aboard, because for the first time in three years she was not the only person acting as though the thing she had heard was real.
On the ninth day, Halloway found the first hole.
"This is not an error," the purser said, "and I want that understood, because I have found four thousand errors in this ledger and I know what an error looks like. This is not one."
He had eleven sheets in front of him. On each, a single line was ringed in his very small, very neat pencil.

"Twelve years ago, the Gull came into Antrell for her long refit. Two hundred and eleven days out of service. During a refit the bells are not rung, because the ship is on the cradles and there is nothing to hold up. The tally is closed. Look."
He turned a sheet. The lines stopped. A clerk's hand had written, on the last line: TALLY CLOSED — REFIT — REOPEN ON UNDOCK.

"And here is the reopening, two hundred and eleven days later. In a different hand, which is correct, because the bell-master changed during the refit. And here — " his pencil moved " — is the first round of the new run, and the Ninth is marked thin. And here is the second, thin. And the third, and the fourth. Thin, thin, thin, for nineteen days, and then it goes full and stays full for eleven years, and I would have called that a bell settling after a refit and thought no more about it."
"So would I," said Roake, quietly.

"Except." Halloway spread the eleven sheets. "Except that on each of these eleven days, spread across eleven years, the Ninth goes dead for exactly one round and then comes back. Not thin. Dead. One round, once, and back to full. Eleven times in eleven years, and here is the part I dislike: it is always the third watch, and it is always within a day of the ship passing the same point on the crossing."
Dov leaned over the sheets so fast he knocked a lamp. "Which point?"

Halloway put his pencil down on the chart, on a patch of the Cloudsea south of the shipping line, an unremarkable stretch of nothing that every ferry on the run went around rather than through, because the air there was dead and would not carry sound, and a ring-ship in dead air is a ship with a mouth full of wool.
The Quiet.
"There is nothing there," said Sol.
"There is nothing there," Halloway agreed, "on our charts."
Nobody said anything for a while. The Gull creaked and hummed and went on holding herself up.
Then Captain Marn, who had come in at some point and had been standing by the door long enough to hear most of it, said:
"Bosun, what is the name of the bell-master who signed the tally open after that refit?"

Roake did not need to look. Sol watched her not need to look, and understood that this was the moment the whole thing had been walking towards since a woman of fourteen heard a bell answer wrong and spent eleven years not saying so.
"Ysolde Kerrin," said Tamsin Roake. "She taught me. She signed my papers. And eleven years ago she went off this ship at Kettlemouth with a crate on a handcart, and nobody has seen her since."
